turns.text: Thanks. Feeling slightly less doomed.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Nobody will mind. Drive safely, the cake isn't going anywhere.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do families usually split wedding costs these days?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There's no single rule anymore. Many couples pay most of it themselves, and parents contribute what they can or want to.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My parents offered a fixed amount. His parents haven't said anything.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's common. You could gently ask if they'd like to help with something specific, like the rehearsal dinner or the flowers.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is that rude?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not if you frame it as an invitation, not a bill. Some parents love having one thing that's theirs.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. And if they say no?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you plan with what you have. And try not to compare, it can create tension that lasts longer than the wedding.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fair. I'll let my fiance ask them, / since they're his parents.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good instinct. It usually goes better coming from their own kid.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: When should save the dates go out?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually about six to eight months before. For a destination wedding, closer to a year so people can save and book.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ours is local, in August.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then sending them in January or February is perfect.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do people still mail them, or is email fine?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Email is totally fine now, especially if you're watching costs. Older relatives might appreciate a paper one though.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My grandma would frame a paper one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then print a handful for the grandparents and email the rest. Everyone's happy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the actual invites?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Around two months before, with an RSVP date about a month before the wedding.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We want a non-religious ceremony. How do we even structure it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A simple shape works well. A welcome from the officiant, a short story about you two, a reading or two, your vows, the rings, and the pronouncement.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The story part sounds nice. Who tells it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually the officiant, using things you've shared with them. How you met, what you love about each other, a funny moment.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can we add something to make it feel like a ritual? / Without it being religious.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sure. Some couples do a handfasting, tying their hands with a ribbon. Others plant a tree or mix two kinds of sand.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Planting something is very us. We met at a garden centre.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then that's perfect. Plant a little tree in a pot during the ceremony and take it home.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I love that.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It gives your guests something to watch, and you something to keep.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm invited to a wedding and I have a serious nut allergy. Is it rude to mention it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not rude at all, it's important. Most RSVP cards or wedding websites have a spot for dietary needs.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: This one just says yes or no.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then send the couple a short message. Keep it light, just say you have a nut allergy and ask who to check with about the menu.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They're stressed enough already.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's why you offer to talk to the caterer directly. It takes the job off their plate.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, smart. Should I bring food just in case?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A small snack in your bag is sensible, plus your medication. Then you can relax and enjoy it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Thanks. I hate being that guest.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You're not that guest, you're being safe. Any good couple would want to know.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is a wedding planner worth the money, honestly?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Depends on your time and stress levels. A full planner can cost a lot, but they know vendors and can save you money and headaches.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We both work long hours and neither of us is organised.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a planner might be worth it. Or a day-of coordinator, who's cheaper and just handles the final month and the day itself.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What does day-of actually mean? Just the one day?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually they start a few weeks before. They confirm vendors, run the schedule and deal with problems so you don't have to.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds like the dream. / My mum will hate it, though, she wanted that job.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Give her a special role then, like greeting guests or the family photos. She'll still feel important.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sneaky. I like it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The wedding's tomorrow and I can't stop shaking.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's completely normal. Have you eaten today?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Barely. Some crackers.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Eat something real tonight, and drink water. Nerves get worse on an empty stomach.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My head is full of everything that could go wrong.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Things might go a little wrong, and nobody will notice. Guests remember how happy you looked, not whether the napkins matched.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That actually helps.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Also, pick one person to handle problems tomorrow. Anything goes wrong, they deal with it, not you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My sister would love that power.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect. Give her the job, then go to bed early. You've done the work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What do I write in a wedding card? I've been staring at it for ten minutes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with a simple wish, then add something personal. How well do you know them?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The groom's my oldest friend. I barely know her yet.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you could write about him, and how happy he seems with her. That welcomes her in too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like, I've never seen him smile this much?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly that kind of thing. Then end with something warm, like wishing them a lifetime of adventures.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I add a joke? We have a lot of inside jokes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe one small one, if she'd get it. Save the rest for your speech, or for later.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I think I can write it now.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You've got it. Honest beats clever every time.

option_sets.lead_in: We've narrowed the venue down and I need a second opinion.
options: The first one is an old barn on a farm, really charming, but there's no air conditioning.
Then there's a hotel ballroom downtown, very easy for guests, though it feels a bit generic.
And the last option is a vineyard about an hour out of town, stunning views, but the most expensive.
moshi_comment: The vineyard sounds the most memorable, but an hour's drive can be tough for older guests. The hotel is the practical choice, especially if lots of people are traveling in. When is the wedding?
If it's a summer wedding, I'd worry about the barn without air conditioning. Between the other two, it comes down to whether views or convenience matter more to you.

option_sets.lead_in: I can't decide what to do about catering for the reception.
options: One idea is a classic plated dinner, chicken or fish, served at the tables.
Another is a big buffet with a bit of everything, which is cheaper per person.
There's also a couple of food trucks, tacos and pizza, parked outside the venue.
And finally, my aunt offered to cook everything herself for free.
moshi_comment: Food trucks are fun and relaxed, and guests usually love them, but lines can get long with a big crowd. The plated dinner feels the most formal. How many guests are you expecting?
Your aunt's offer is generous, but cooking for a whole reception is a huge job on the day itself. I'd lean toward the buffet, it's flexible and cheaper than a plated dinner.

option_sets.lead_in: We need music for the reception and I'm torn.
options: A live band that plays covers, they're brilliant but they cost about as much as the catering.
A DJ who's done loads of weddings at the venue and knows how to get the grandparents dancing.
Or our own playlist on a speaker, basically free, with a friend in charge of the volume.
moshi_comment: A band brings huge energy, but it's a big chunk of the budget. The DJ is the safe middle, especially since they know the venue, and I'd only do the playlist if your crowd is pretty low-key.
If dancing is the heart of the night, the DJ who reads the room is hard to beat. The band is the luxury choice, and the playlist risks awkward gaps unless your friend is really on it.

option_sets.lead_in: I've tried on dresses all weekend and I'm stuck between a few.
options: A fitted lace dress with long sleeves, very elegant, but I can barely sit down in it.
A flowy chiffon one with an open back that moves beautifully, though my mum calls it a nightgown.
A simple satin slip dress that I could probably wear again, and it's half the price of the others.
And a big ballgown my sister picked, which made everyone in the shop cry.
moshi_comment: You'll be in it for twelve hours, so the lace one worries me if you can't sit. The chiffon sounds comfortable and stunning, mums come around. The ballgown clearly had a moment, but did you feel like yourself in it?
The satin slip is the practical star, simple and wearable again. If you want the wow, it's the ballgown or the chiffon. I'd pick whichever you kept thinking about on the drive home.

option_sets.lead_in: The venue gave us three possible dates and we have to pick by Friday.
options: A Saturday in late June, peak season and perfect weather, but it's the most expensive.
A Friday in September, cheaper and still warm, but some guests would need a day off work.
A Sunday in early December, half the price and cosy, though it's close to the holidays.
moshi_comment: June is the dream if the budget allows, but September is often just as lovely and much cheaper. I'd worry about December, people's calendars get crowded then.
The September Friday is the sweet spot for me, good weather and a real saving, and most people will happily take a day off for a wedding. December can be beautiful, just less predictable for travel.
